amendments.rule: A verbless clause supplies its English copula from the construction, not from nothing. In *that it was good*, the supplied *it was* belongs to the unit headed on `טוֹב`; do not mark it `added`. **Where the ASV renders a verbless clause with a presentative *there was* or *there were*, the dummy *there* is part of the same construction-supplied frame as the copula and joins the unit that bears that copula under this rule.** It is never `added`, and the unit still heads on its lexical predicate or anchor. **The anchor may be of any kind, since what licenses the dummy is the presentative frame the construction supplies and not the part of speech the frame is built on.** A nominal anchor, a prepositional predicate and an adverbial anchor are read alike: `וְעוֹד חָמֵשְׁ שָׁנִים` → *and* ***there are yet*** *five years* gives *there are yet* to `עוֹד`, headed on *yet*, and the numeral phrase keeps its own English. Do not read the list as closed and mark the dummy `added` because the anchor is neither a noun nor a preposition; the sentence above says it is never `added`, and rule 17 puts the same dummy on a finite verb and rule 50 on an existential `אַיִן`. **But the dummy this sentence governs is the presentative *there* and no other.** A cleft or impersonal *it* the ASV writes in such a clause — *it was not you that sent me hither*, *It is enough* — is not a presentative frame and no morpheme licenses it, so it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, exactly as the supplied lexical verb of the next sentence is. **Apart from that presentative dummy, this covers the copula and nothing more.** Where the ASV instead supplies a whole *lexical* verb for a clause whose Hebrew has none — the allotment formula `וְלִבְנֵי קְהָת הַנּוֹתָרִים ... עָרִים עָשֶׂר` → *And unto the rest of the sons of Kohath* ***were given*** *by lot ... ten cities* — no morpheme's rendering that verb completes, and it is `added` under rule 30, together with any object the ASV supplies alongside it, as in *were given them*. Test by asking which morpheme is there to carry the English: `הָיָה` carries the *have* of rule 43 and the frame of rule 21, a Hebrew verb carries the light verb of rule 44, and a preposition that is itself the predicate carries the copula of rule 49 — but a preposition the ASV has already spent a word on, as in *unto the rest*, carries nothing further, and a clause with no verb in it at all licenses no verb. **But the copula is whatever verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand, and not the word *be* alone.** English links a subject to its predicate with *seem*, *become*, *prove*, *remain* and *come* as readily as with *be*, and such a verb is the construction-supplied copula of this rule rather than a supplied lexical verb: it joins the unit of the predicate morpheme it links, which keeps its own English beside it, and that unit still heads on the word carrying the predicate's lexeme under rule 24 rather than on the linking verb. `וּגְדוֹלָה הִיא אֵלָי` → *and it* ***seemed*** *great unto me* gives *seemed great* to `גָּדוֹל`, headed on *great*, while `הִיא` keeps only its own *it*; `הַכֹּל כַּאֲשֶׁר לַכֹּל` → *All things* ***come*** *alike to all* gives *come alike* to the `כַּאֲשֶׁר` that is the clause's predicate, headed on *alike*. This is rule 49's reading of `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which* ***belonged to*** *the house* and of a resultative `לְ` → *shalt become*, holding for a predicate of any kind and not only a prepositional one, and rule 30 already states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of a fused expression does not defeat its one-rendering condition. What tells such a verb from the supplied lexical verb of the preceding sentences is whether a predicate morpheme stands in the clause for it to link: a linking verb stands beside that predicate's own English and adds no participant the Hebrew does not write, whereas *were given* introduces an event and an agent the Hebrew never wrote, and rule 34's *cheweth* stands in a line whose predicate the Hebrew leaves unwritten altogether. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do — drop the English verb and ask whether what has gone is the link English writes for a predication the Hebrew already made, or the predication itself. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **A tripartite clause whose resuming pronoun the ASV renders by nothing but that copula is read on those same terms.** Where the clause writes a subject noun and resumes it with `הוּא`, `הִיא` or `הֵמָּה` before the predicate, and the ASV realizes the subject once by the noun, the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, while the copula joins the predicate as the preceding sentences direct, discontinuous around a possessive or an article under rule 25: `יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ` → *Jehovah* ***is*** *their* ***inheritance*** gives *is inheritance* to `נַחֲלָה` and leaves `הוּא` nothing. Do not give the copula to that pronoun on the ground that a present morpheme takes its English before a construction-supplied reading: what that reasoning governs, in rules 46, 47 and 48, is an English word some morpheme's own sense answers to, and a copula answers to the predication rather than to the pronoun, which is why this rule sends it to the predicate wherever a predicate morpheme stands. Where instead the ASV writes a word of its own for the pronoun — `הוּא הַדָּבָר` → ***that*** *is the thing* — that pronoun is holding an English word already and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and the copula still joins the predicate. One chapter may write both shapes, and DEU.18.2 and DEU.18.22 do. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.
amendments.why: The chapter met the same construction twice and split on it, which is the sign of a gap rather than of a bad verse pass. Rule 20's sentence 'this covers the copula and nothing more' reads naturally as covering *be* and nothing else, so ECC.9.13's *seemed* was folded into the predicate adjective while ECC.9.2's *come* was marked `added` as a supplied lexical verb, though both clauses write their own predicate and neither verb adds a participant. The contract already gives a non-*be* frame to a predicate morpheme in rule 49 — *belonged to*, *shalt become*, *shall be turned into* — but only for a prepositional predicate, so nothing covered an adjectival or particle predicate. The amendment states the boundary where rule 20 draws it, keeps its existing lexical-verb examples intact by naming what distinguishes them (a new event with its own participants, or a line whose predicate the Hebrew leaves unwritten), and adds the subtraction test the rest of the contract uses. It narrows nothing: the allotment formula, the *done* of a nominal recasting and rule 34's *cheweth* all still fall on the `added` side by the test as written.

conventions: Comparative clauses: where the Hebrew writes the adjective (9.4, 9.16, 9.18), that adjective takes the construction-supplied copula together with *better* and the comparative preposition keeps only its own *than*. Where the Hebrew writes no adjective at all and the comparison rests on the preposition alone (9.17), the preposition is the clause's predicate and takes the whole supplied frame *are better than* under rule 49, headed on *than*; *better* is not `added` there, because dropping it leaves the preposition with no rendering. Heading such a unit on *better* is the named competing reading.

The focus particle used correlatively is a connective of its own for rule 14's purposes. Where the chapter writes the particle once per member (9.1 *whether ... or*, 9.6 *As well ... as ... and*), each occurrence takes only the English connective the ASV wrote for its own member, and no occurrence takes the pair; the reading that gives an opening correlative such as *whether* or *As well* to one particle and leaves the other `unrepresented` was rejected.

Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.
amended.why: The chapter met the same construction twice and split on it, which is the sign of a gap rather than of a bad verse pass. Rule 20's sentence 'this covers the copula and nothing more' reads naturally as covering *be* and nothing else, so ECC.9.13's *seemed* was folded into the predicate adjective while ECC.9.2's *come* was marked `added` as a supplied lexical verb, though both clauses write their own predicate and neither verb adds a participant. The contract already gives a non-*be* frame to a predicate morpheme in rule 49 — *belonged to*, *shalt become*, *shall be turned into* — but only for a prepositional predicate, so nothing covered an adjectival or particle predicate. The amendment states the boundary where rule 20 draws it, keeps its existing lexical-verb examples intact by naming what distinguishes them (a new event with its own participants, or a line whose predicate the Hebrew leaves unwritten), and adds the subtraction test the rest of the contract uses. It narrows nothing: the allotment formula, the *done* of a nominal recasting and rule 34's *cheweth* all still fall on the `added` side by the test as written.

report: One real split, ECC.9.2 against ECC.9.13: a verbless clause for which the ASV supplies an English linking verb other than *be*. ECC.9.13 gives *seemed* to the predicate adjective as the construction-supplied copula (rule 20); ECC.9.2 marked *come* `added` as a supplied lexical verb, though its clause likewise writes its own predicate (the particle rendered *alike*) and the verb only links the subject to it. Nothing in the source licenses the difference, only which English verb the ASV chose. Patched ECC.9.2 to read the compound particle as *come alike*, one unit headed on the preposition and on *alike*; ECC.9.13 stands unchanged.

Not splits, checked and left alone. The comparative family (9.4, 9.16, 9.18 against 9.17): where a written adjective stands, it takes *is better* and the comparative preposition keeps only *than*; at 9.17 no adjective stands in the Hebrew, so the preposition is itself the clause's predicate and takes *are better than* under rule 49, headed on *than*. The correlative particle series (9.1 *whether ... or*, 9.6 *As well ... as ... and*): each written particle takes the one connective the ASV wrote for its own member, which is rule 14's ruling for a Hebrew that writes a connective per member, not one morpheme holding a correlative pair. The two occurrences of the compound particle in 9.2 differ because the second is a preposition plus a headless relative with an English word for each morpheme (rule 2), while the first is the fixed particle rendered by one word.

Also checked and consistent across the chapter: the existential negative heads on its negation word in all five occurrences, with its suffix `unrepresented` wherever the ASV writes no separate subject pronoun (9.2, 9.5, 9.16); the possessive preposition plus suffix of 9.5 and 9.6 takes *have* plus *they* alike (rule 43); waw plus negative fuses to *nor*/*neither* in 9.11 where a negative is written, while 9.10's waws take *nor* alone under the single existential's scope, which is rule 35's own instruction to align what is actually there; the article on the noun for man is bare *man* at 9.1 and 9.12 and takes the fronted *the* in the construct chains of 9.3 and 9.12; the object marker is `unrepresented` in six places and takes *to* only at 9.11, where the English verb reaches its object through it (rule 16's first family).

BSB: 18 disagreements, none a genuine error. Ten are the documented article convention. The rest are the ASV recastings rule 40 silences (9.4 dative, 9.8 locative, 9.9 dative), rule 20's tripartite resuming pronoun at 9.4, the unrendered existential suffixes at 9.2, 9.5 and 9.16 (rules 22, 50), and the one surplus waw of 9.2, where four written *and*s are counted against five waws by the members each stands between (rule 42). No accepted edge was changed to improve the rate.
Two conventions recorded, and rule 20 amended so the linking-verb boundary is stated where a later pass will read it rather than left to be rediscovered.
